opus-5.5.text:
That's a really interesting question, and I think it gets at one of the most fundamental differences between working on robotics and working on language models.

With a large language model, the thinking-time budget is quite flexible. If you ask a model a hard math problem or a coding question, it's perfectly acceptable for it to think for ten seconds, thirty seconds, even several minutes. The world waits for it. Nothing bad happens while it's reasoning. That's why we've seen this whole trend of test-time compute, chain of thought, letting the model think longer to get better answers. Time is relatively cheap.

For a robot, the world doesn't wait. If a robot is walking and it starts to slip, it has maybe tens of milliseconds to react. If it's catching an object or handing something to a person, the physical dynamics are unfolding in real time. You simply cannot pause the world and say, "Let me think about this for a minute." So at the lowest level of control, the budget is extremely tight, often requiring decisions at tens or hundreds of hertz.

But I don't think it's purely that robots must think fast. What we've found is that robotics actually needs both. There's a hierarchy. At the high level, if a robot is asked to clean up a kitchen or pack a lunch box, it's fine to spend a few seconds planning: understanding the scene, figuring out the sequence of steps, reasoning about what goes where. That part looks a lot like a language model, and it can benefit from the same kind of deliberate reasoning. At the low level, the motor control, the reactive behaviors, has to be fast, almost reflexive.

This is a bit like how humans work, the "thinking fast and slow" idea. When you walk down the street, you're not consciously reasoning about each footstep. But when you decide which route to take, you can stop and think. A good robot system needs that same structure: a slower, more deliberate reasoning layer, and a fast, reactive control layer underneath.

So the challenge for us is figuring out how to bring the power of large models, which are typically big and slow, into a system that must act in real time. That's driven a lot of work on things like separating the reasoning model from the action model, distilling large models into smaller ones that can run on the robot, and designing the interface between the slow brain and the fast body. I think getting that balance right is one of the key open problems in embodied AI right now.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts LLM answers that can take seconds or minutes with robot actions that may need reactions within tens of milliseconds, clearly stating robots have a much shorter per-action thinking-time budget.

fable-5.1.text:
That's actually one of the most fundamental differences, and I think people who come from the language model side often underestimate it.

With a large language model, you can afford to think. If a user asks a hard math question, the model can spend thirty seconds, a minute, even several minutes generating chain-of-thought, and the user will wait. The world is paused while the model thinks. Nothing bad happens during that time. So the whole test-time compute paradigm, where you scale up reasoning tokens to get better answers, works beautifully, because latency is almost free.

A robot doesn't have that luxury. The world doesn't pause. If a quadruped is walking down stairs and its foot slips, it has maybe fifty to a hundred milliseconds to react before it falls. A humanoid balancing on one leg needs to send motor commands at hundreds of hertz. You cannot say "hold on, let me reason about this for ten seconds." By then you're on the floor.

So in robotics we end up with this very layered picture of time. At the bottom you have the low-level controller, which runs at maybe 500 or 1,000 hertz and has essentially zero thinking budget. It's reflexive. It's closer to the spinal cord than to the brain. Above that you have something like a locomotion or manipulation policy, which might run at 50 hertz. And then at the top, you can have a language model or a VLA doing high-level planning at maybe one hertz, or even slower, deciding "go to the kitchen, pick up the cup."

What's interesting is that this is actually very similar to how biology handles it. Humans also have fast reflexes and slow deliberation, and most of what we do in the physical world is not deliberate at all. You don't consciously think about how to place your foot.

So my view is that we shouldn't try to make one model do everything at one speed. The big model should be allowed to think slowly, and we should design the system so that its slowness is hidden behind fast, robust low-level control. The hard research question is the interface between those layers: how does the slow thinker hand off to the fast reactor in a way where the fast part can still be safe and competent when the slow part hasn't finished thinking yet?

And honestly, I think robotics will push language models in a good direction here, because it forces us to ask: what's the minimum amount of thinking needed to act well right now, rather than how much thinking can we afford.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts users waiting seconds or minutes for an LLM with robots needing to react within milliseconds or hundreds of hertz while the world continues moving.

astra-6.text:
I think the key difference is that a robot’s thinking-time budget is imposed by the physical world. A language model can often spend more time reasoning, and the tradeoff is that the user waits longer. But if a robot is losing its balance, it can’t say, “Give me another ten seconds to think.” By then, it has already fallen.

So for robots, we need to think about intelligence at different timescales. Planning a task can take longer, but reacting to contact or maintaining balance has to happen very quickly. You might have a slower reasoning system deciding what to do and a fast controller handling how to move.

That also means a better answer delivered too late can be worse than a good-enough answer delivered on time. For a robot, timing is part of correctness.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts language models’ ability to spend more time while users wait with robots’ need to react very quickly per action; it says a robot cannot take another ten seconds when losing balance. This clearly communicates a much shorter action-time budget than users will tolerate for an LLM answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is that a robot has to operate on the clock of the physical world. If it’s losing its balance, it may have only milliseconds to react. It can’t say, “Let me think for another minute,” because by then it has already fallen.

For a language model, there’s often more flexibility. If you ask a difficult question, waiting a few extra seconds—or even minutes—can be worthwhile if it produces a better answer. With robots, a better answer that arrives too late can be useless.

So I think robots need different levels of thinking. Fast control has to run continuously, while slower reasoning can handle things like planning a route or deciding how to approach a task. The challenge is connecting those levels so the robot can think carefully without stopping its ability to react.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a robot’s millisecond-scale reaction deadline with the extra seconds or minutes users may wait for a language model answer, clearly conveying that robots need much shorter thinking times per action.
